title: Assange's release won't stop government lies
subtitle: The paradox of speaking truth to power
author: Sophie Scott-Brown
introduction: Whilst the release of Julian Assange has been celebrated by his friends, family and defenders, the powers that imprisoned him remain unconstrained. Is his release a victory and for whom? While acknowledging Assange's role in exposing harsh war truths, Sophie Scott-Brown argues that "speaking truth to power" now reinforces the power structures it seeks to challenge. Scott-Brown calls for a society of shared responsibilities, free from permanent authorities, especially in light of current global crises.
body:
Assange’s release is welcome news, but is it really a victory? And if so, of what for whom?  Assange forced on us the painful, undeniable facts proving what most people dimly suspected but didn’t want to know, that appalling things are done by all sides in a war. In doing so, he joined a select elite of people who have sacrificed themselves—their time, liberty, health, and often lives—to ‘speak truth to power.’

Belief that displacing illusion and superstition with facts and reason ensures prosperity is the bedrock of modern liberal faith.

This idea—speaking truth to power—fascinates and repels us. Its roots lie deep in religious dissent and those heretics prepared to oppose religious establishment, the state, and the law in the name of divine truth (or their version of it). While the element of martyrdom remains, the secular version, as embodied by the Enlightenment, prevails now. Belief that displacing illusion and superstition with facts and reason ensures prosperity is the bedrock of modern liberal faith.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Dangerous media for dangerous times With Matt Kelly, Alan Rusbridger

In another sense, however, this idea is naïve and reinforces the same power it claims to challenge. It does this by massaging two long standing myths: first, that authority is a necessary evil protecting us from others and ourselves, and second, that it helps us collectively progress. Inspired by these principles, how much effort has gone into theorising ideal leaders, perfect governments, foolproof judiciaries in the hopes that, if properly implemented, they will fulfil these objectives? If anything errs it is not because of authority per-se, but because someone or something is not following the plan. As citizens, our primary jobs are to be to be vigilant, to point out ‘errors’ when we see them, and to waggle our fingers at them.

It just exchanges multiple small bullies for one super-bully.

Yet if we pause for a moment, it’s clear neither claim makes sense. Supposing we do need protection and regulation because we are all self-interested, how, then, does giving an individual or small group of individuals increased capacity to enforce their will over others solve that problem? It just exchanges multiple small bullies for one super-bully. Similarly, if progress means our ability to live well in safety, that is incompatible with maintaining a permanent authority which is defined by and dependent on the use of force to hold power.

There is a disconnect, then, between what we claim for power and how it works. What’s more, anyone in power understands that (and doesn’t last long if they don’t). But, if, as Noam Chomsky once said, power already knows the truth and is busy disguising it, does that make Assange’s 14 years in captivity meaningless? It may be that Assange and others like him are not really speaking to power at all, but to us, the easily beguiled public. Perhaps their sacrifice is to show us what power really is and make us confront the truth we already know to be true. Fine, but, even if we are now all caught up, so what? Are we condemned to collectively shaking our fist but nothing more, or are there things we can do?

SUGGESTED VIEWING Fascist passions With Judith Butler

Let’s say we bracket our concerns and try to make the myths work; do we have anything like the tools for holding power to account? Assange proved America’s ‘foul play’ in the Iraq conflict, but what can be done about that? We might be tempted to point to the United Nations or the International Criminal Court for answers but how effective are these organisations? Again, the flaw is in-built and inescapable. The UN, for example, derives what authority it has from being a members’ organisation, an exemplary model of deliberative decision making among national representatives, but this poses an instant conundrum. Any motion carried has power because most members have agreed to it but to reach that point, whatever is proposed must be sufficiently inoffensive to carry the majority with it.

We need to be more imaginative. I don’t want more martyrs like Assange, I want to be part of a society of free, equal people sharing responsibility for the difficult daily business of living together. Instead of wasting energy regulating and subduing a guardian we can’t trust and don’t need, we should focus, instead, on finding ways of living together that neither assume nor depend on permanent authority. Once upon a time, this might have sounded utopian, but now, as environmental collapse, advancing AI, and perpetual conflict re-write what it means to be alive, we can no longer afford to defer our decisions to others.
